newsitem.title: UK: Majority of UK business leaders oppose EMU - poll.
newsitem.headline: Majority of UK business leaders oppose EMU - poll.

text.p: Nearly 60 percent of British company directors oppose a single European currency on the grounds that it would be bad for the economy, according to an opinion poll published on Monday.
The poll of 392 directors of listed companies by Hemmington Scott for accountants Price Waterhouse showed 58.4 percent opposed to monetary union, while 4.4 percent reserved judgment.

"Even among the 37.2 percent who support the idea, there are plenty who think Britain should exercise its opt-out clause and postpone adoption of the Euro beyond 1999," Hemmington Scott said. There are 1,751 companies listed on the UK stock exchange.

More than 57 percent of those surveyed thought taxes would go up, 42 percent expected government borrowing to soar, 40.8 percent believed prices would rise and 39.5 percent expected interest rates to increase.
Commenting on the survey, Helen Kay of Hemmington Scott said,

"Whether they object on intellectual or emotional grounds (or a mixture of the two), it is abundantly obvious from their responses that the majority of the industrialists who participated in our poll oppose both the introduction of the Euro and the federalisation they worry will follow in its wake."

Hemmington Scott said 57.6 percent of respondents expected a single currency would lead to greater unemployment while 64.2 percent feared it would increase pressure for subsidies to poorer member states.

More than half of those surveyed thought a single currency would reduce London's ability to remain Europe's financial centre, while 66.3 percent thought the City's financial power would be eroded by the creation of an independent European central bank.

Almost 60 percent of respondents did not believe the long-term benefits of a single currency would justify the costs of adapting Britain's financial systems or the transitional costs companies would incur.
"On the key issue of sovereignty, 73.9 percent ot those surveyed believe monetary union would erode Britain's national identity," Hemmington Scott said.
